title: Daguerre's Mirror with a Memory
summary: Louis Daguerre was a Paris showman who painted giant scenes that seemed to come alive with light. After his partner Niépce died, he found a way to make photographs on shiny silver plates in minutes instead of hours. In 1839 France gave his invention to the whole world, and soon everyone wanted their portrait taken.

sections.heading: The Showman of the Diorama
paragraphs: Picture yourself in Paris in the 1820s, buying a ticket to the most talked-about show in town. You walk down a dark corridor and step into a round, dim room with a few hundred other people. Ahead of you, through a great opening about seven metres wide and six metres tall, you see a mountain valley in Switzerland. As you watch, the light slowly changes. Clouds seem to drift, the sky darkens, and the valley sinks into evening. Then, with a low rumble, the whole room you are standing in turns slowly on a giant turntable, and a second scene swings into view: a ruined chapel, perhaps, with moonlight falling through its broken windows.

This was the Diorama, and the man behind it was Louis-Jacques-Mandé Daguerre. Daguerre was born on 18 November 1787 in Cormeilles-en-Parisis, a village near Paris. As a young man he trained in architecture and theatre design, and he worked as an assistant to Pierre Prévost, a painter of panoramas, the enormous 360-degree paintings that surrounded viewers in a circular building. Daguerre became a celebrated designer of stage scenery for Paris theatres, famous for clever lighting effects.

In 1821 he teamed up with another painter, Charles-Marie Bouton, and in 1822 they opened the Diorama in Paris. The trick lay in how the pictures were painted. Each scene was painted on huge sheets of linen, and some areas were painted so that they were partly see-through. Light could shine onto the front of the painting or through it from behind, controlled by skylights, shutters, screens and coloured blinds. By slowly changing which light was used, the operators could make day turn into night, or make a lamp glow in a window that had seemed dark. Each scene lasted about 10 to 15 minutes, and up to about 350 people at a time stood or sat on the turning floor.

Audiences were amazed, and many people believed they were looking at a real landscape. One of Daguerre's scenes, the Interior of Roslin Chapel in Scotland, was shown in Paris in the 1820s, and The Times newspaper in London later called it 'perfectly magical'. The Diorama was so popular that a second one opened in London's Regent's Park in 1823, and others followed in Berlin and elsewhere. At its height, Daguerre's Paris Diorama is said to have earned about 200,000 francs a year.

Notice what Daguerre's whole career was about: realistic images, light, and wowing a crowd. He spent his days thinking about how light falls on things and how to fool the eye into seeing reality. It is no wonder that, like many painters of his time, he used a camera obscura to help with his drawings, and wished its glowing image could somehow be kept. That wish is what led him to Niépce, and to the partnership you read about in the last part.

sections.heading: Alone in the Workshop: The Hidden Picture
paragraphs: When Niépce died in 1833, Daguerre carried on, working with Niépce's son Isidore as his new partner on paper, but mostly experimenting on his own. He focused on silver. He took a sheet of copper coated with a thin layer of silver and polished it until it shone like a mirror. Then he held the plate over iodine, a chemical whose purple vapour reacts with silver to form a pale yellow coating of silver iodide, a light-sensitive substance.

Silver iodide darkens in light, but slowly. If Daguerre waited until a visible picture appeared in his camera, it still took far too long. The great breakthrough, probably made around 1835, was the discovery of the latent image. 'Latent' means hidden. Daguerre found that after a much shorter exposure, when the plate still looked completely blank, light had already left an invisible trace in the silver iodide. If he then treated the plate with the right chemical, that hidden picture could be brought out, or developed, into a visible one.

The chemical he used was mercury, the silvery liquid metal once used in thermometers. When a plate was held over a dish of gently heated mercury, the mercury vapour settled on the places where light had struck and formed tiny, bright, whitish grains there. The more light a spot had received, the more mercury gathered on it. Slowly, as if by magic, a sharp, detailed picture appeared on the blank silver.

There is a famous story about how Daguerre found this out. According to the tale, he put an under-exposed plate away in a cupboard full of chemicals, and when he took it out a few days later, a picture had mysteriously appeared. He then removed the chemicals one by one until he realised that the culprit was mercury from a broken thermometer. It is a lovely story, but it is a legend. Modern historians have found no reliable evidence for it and think it was invented later to make the discovery sound more dramatic. Discoveries in chemistry usually come from long, patient experiments, and Daguerre's almost certainly did too.

There was still one problem: the plate had to be made permanent. Unused silver iodide would keep darkening in light and slowly ruin the picture. In 1837 Daguerre found that he could stop this by washing the plate in a hot, strong solution of ordinary table salt, which dissolved away most of the remaining light-sensitive silver. That year he made a still life of plaster casts, a wicker-covered bottle and other objects in a corner of his studio, which is one of the oldest surviving daguerreotypes. He named his new process the daguerreotype, after himself, and began looking for a way to make money from it.

sections.heading: How to Make a Daguerreotype, Step by Step
paragraphs: Making a daguerreotype was a little like following a difficult cooking recipe in which several of the ingredients were dangerous. Here is how a photographer in the early 1840s would have done it.

Step one: polish the plate. The photographer took a copper plate coated with silver and buffed it again and again with soft cloths and fine powders such as rottenstone and jeweller's rouge, until the silver was a flawless mirror. Any scratch or fingerprint would show up in the final picture. Some photographers also wiped the plate with a little weak nitric acid to clean it.

Step two: make it sensitive. In a dim room, the plate was placed face down over a box containing iodine crystals. The iodine vapour turned the silver surface a golden yellow colour. After 1840, photographers learned to add a second fuming with bromine or chlorine, which made the plate much more sensitive to light and greatly cut exposure times.

Step three: expose it. The plate, protected in a light-tight holder, was slipped into the camera. The photographer removed the lens cap, counted the seconds or minutes, and put the cap back. In 1839 a sunny outdoor view needed several minutes. Later, with better plates and lenses, a portrait in a bright studio could take just a few seconds to under a minute.

Step four: develop it. In the dark, the plate was placed at an angle in a box above a small dish of mercury, which was warmed by a spirit lamp underneath. Over several minutes, the mercury vapour brought out the hidden image. Through a small yellow window in the box, the photographer could watch the picture appear.

Step five: fix it. Daguerre first used hot salt water, but within a year or so most photographers switched to a chemical nicknamed 'hypo' (sodium thiosulfate), which dissolved the leftover silver iodide far better. You will meet the scientist behind hypo in the next part. Step six: protect it. From 1840, many photographers followed the advice of the French physicist Hippolyte Fizeau and gently heated the plate with a gold chloride solution, which made the image richer and tougher. Finally, because the surface could be smudged by the lightest touch, the plate was sealed behind glass and put in a small hinged case, often lined with velvet.

sections.heading: Free to the World
paragraphs: Daguerre had a wonderful invention, but he had a business problem. If he sold the method to one customer, that customer could simply tell everybody else, and the secret would be gone. He tried to sell shares in the process by subscription, but not enough people signed up. So he turned to one of the most famous scientists in France for help.

François Arago was director of the Paris Observatory, a leading physicist and astronomer, permanent secretary of the French Academy of Sciences, and also a member of the French parliament, the Chamber of Deputies. Daguerre showed him the process under a promise of secrecy, and Arago was thrilled. He saw at once how useful it could be for science: for copying ancient inscriptions, for astronomy, for making accurate maps and drawings. He decided France should buy the invention and give it away.

On 7 January 1839, Arago stood before the members of the French Academy of Sciences and told them about Daguerre's discovery. He described what the pictures looked like and how amazingly detailed they were, but he did not reveal the method. News spread quickly. Within days, newspapers across Europe were reporting that a Frenchman could make nature draw its own portrait in a few minutes. Many people could hardly believe it.

Then came the politics. Arago and others persuaded the French government to make a deal. Daguerre would receive a pension of 6,000 francs a year for the rest of his life, and Isidore Niépce, representing his father's share, would receive 4,000 francs a year. Part of Daguerre's larger pension is said to have been a reward for also revealing how he made his Diorama effects. In return, the full process would be published for anyone to use. The law was passed during the summer of 1839.

On 19 August 1839, at a crowded joint meeting of the Academy of Sciences and the Academy of Fine Arts in Paris, Arago explained the full method in detail. The French government declared it a gift 'free to the world'. Crowds gathered outside the building, eager for news. Within hours, opticians' shops in Paris were reportedly selling out of lenses and chemicals as people rushed to try it themselves.

There was one curious exception to 'free to the world'. A few days before the August announcement, Daguerre's agent, a man named Miles Berry, quietly took out a patent in England. That meant people in England and Wales had to pay a licence fee to make daguerreotypes, while photographers almost everywhere else could use it freely. It was a reminder that even a gift to the world could come with a little fine print.

sections.heading: Daguerreotypomania!
paragraphs: Daguerre quickly published a manual explaining his process, with drawings of the equipment. It was translated into many languages and reprinted again and again within months. In Paris, the firm of Alphonse Giroux began selling a complete official daguerreotype outfit: a big wooden sliding box camera with a lens, plus boxes for coating and developing, bottles of chemicals and everything else needed. It was heavy and expensive, but it is often called the first camera made for sale to the public.

Paris went wild. People carried cameras to bridges and boulevards and pointed them at famous buildings. A French cartoonist, Théodore Maurisset, drew a famous comic picture called 'La Daguerréotypomanie', meaning 'Daguerreotype mania', showing crowds rushing to buy cameras, people queuing for portraits and even gallows for sale to engravers, who joked that they would soon be out of work. The joke had a point. Painters of miniature portraits were indeed among those who lost business as photography spread.

The craze leapt across the Atlantic almost immediately. One of the first Americans to hear about it was Samuel Morse, the painter and inventor who later became famous for the telegraph and Morse code. Morse was in Paris in early 1839 and visited Daguerre, who showed him his pictures. Morse wrote home in amazement, and his letter was published in New York newspapers. Around the same time, disaster struck: on 8 March 1839 a fire broke out at the Diorama, destroying the theatre and many of his paintings. Luckily, much of his photographic equipment and notes were saved.

By the end of 1839, people were experimenting with daguerreotypes in Britain, the United States, Germany, Russia and beyond. Scientists used them to record the Moon, microscopic specimens and, in 1851, a total solar eclipse. Travellers carried them to Egypt to photograph the pyramids and ancient monuments. A new way of seeing the world had arrived.

sections.heading: The First People Caught on a Plate
paragraphs: One of the most famous of Daguerre's own pictures was taken from a window of his studio near the Diorama, looking down on one of the busiest streets in Paris, the Boulevard du Temple. It was made around eight o'clock one spring morning, usually dated to 1838. The street would have been full of carriages, carts, horses and walkers. But in the picture, the boulevard looks strangely empty, like a ghost town.

Why? Because the exposure lasted several minutes. Every carriage that rolled past and every person who strolled by moved too fast to leave a clear image. They passed through the scene like ghosts and vanished. Only things that stayed still were recorded: the buildings, the trees, the pavement.

But look down at the lower left corner of the picture. On the pavement, there is a small dark figure of a man standing with one leg raised, resting his foot on something. He seems to be having his boots shined, and a second, blurrier figure near him may be the bootblack doing the polishing. The customer stood still long enough, while his boots were being cleaned, to become part of history. This tiny figure is often called the first photograph of a living person. (Some researchers have wondered whether the bootblack is really a water pump, and there may be other faint figures, but the customer is clearly a person.)

Daguerre made at least three views of the boulevard that day, in the morning, at noon and in the evening. In October 1839, two of them were set into a frame and presented as a gift to King Ludwig I of Bavaria. The plates later went to a museum in Munich, where they were damaged over the years, especially during a failed restoration attempt in the 1970s. Luckily, the American photography historian Beaumont Newhall had photographed them in the 1930s, so good copies survive. The man with his shined boots never knew he had become the first famous unknown person in photography.

In Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, a young man named Robert Cornelius heard about the daguerreotype in 1839. He worked in his father's company, which made lamps and polished metal fittings, so he knew a lot about silver plating and chemistry. Around October 1839, he set up a homemade camera outside the family shop, removed the lens cap, ran into the frame and sat very still for a long time, possibly as long as ten to fifteen minutes. Then he ran back and covered the lens.

The result is one of the most charming pictures in history. Cornelius, aged about 30, appears slightly off-centre, with his arms crossed and his hair messy, staring at the camera with a mixture of curiosity and seriousness. On the back, he wrote: 'The first light Picture ever taken. 1839.' It may not have been absolutely the first photograph of a person, as you have just seen, but it is one of the earliest photographic portraits of a human being that still exists, and since he took it of himself, it is often called the world's first selfie.

Cornelius did not stop there. Working with a Philadelphia chemist named Paul Beck Goddard, who found ways to make plates more sensitive, he cut portrait exposures to under a minute. In May 1840 he opened one of the earliest photographic portrait studios in the world. A few months earlier, in New York, Alexander Wolcott and John Johnson had opened a studio using a camera with a concave mirror instead of a lens, which gathered more light. Within a couple of years, Cornelius returned to the family lamp business, which earned more money, but his self-portrait made him famous long after his death.

sections.heading: Sit Still! Life in an Early Portrait Studio
paragraphs: Everyone wanted their portrait taken. Before 1839, only fairly well-off people could afford to have a painter make their likeness. A daguerreotype cost money too, but far less than an oil painting, and it was fantastically exact. Soon photographers were opening studios in nearly every city, often on the top floor of a building with large glass windows or skylights, because they needed as much daylight as possible.

In the first years, sitting for a portrait could be hard work. Early lenses were dim, and exposures might last a minute or more. Sitters were told to stay perfectly still. Many studios used a posing stand, a hidden iron brace with a clamp that held the back of the head steady, a little like the neck rest on a dentist's chair. Others had sitters lean on tables or chairs. Parents of small children sometimes hid under a cloth behind the child, holding them steady, a trick that produced what are today called 'hidden mother' photographs.

Technology improved quickly. In 1840, the Hungarian-born mathematician Joseph Petzval designed a new portrait lens that let in many times more light than Daguerre's original lens; the Austrian firm Voigtländer began making it and a compact metal camera to go with it. Together with the extra bromine or chlorine fuming of the plates, the new lenses cut portrait exposures to well under a minute in good light, and sometimes to just a few seconds. That is one reason why the old idea that people in early photos never smiled only because exposures were long is too simple. Holding a smile for a few seconds is easy. Many people looked serious because a portrait was a formal occasion, and because the traditions of painted portraits favoured calm, dignified faces.

The daguerreotype business grew enormous, especially in the United States. By the early 1850s, Americans were making an estimated three million daguerreotypes a year. Famous studios in New York and Boston photographed presidents, writers and ordinary families alike. For the first time, a farmer's family could have an exact image of their grandmother, a soldier could carry a picture of his sweetheart, and grieving parents could keep a picture of a child who had died.

sections.heading: A Mirror That Remembers
paragraphs: If you hold a real daguerreotype in your hand, it feels like holding a tiny, precious mirror. Look at it straight on and you might see only your own reflection. Tilt it slightly against a dark background and the picture leaps out, sharp and silvery, with astonishing detail. Daguerreotypes are so detailed that you can sometimes read shop signs across a street or count the threads in a lace collar with a magnifying glass. An American writer, Oliver Wendell Holmes, later described photography as 'the mirror with a memory', and the phrase fits the daguerreotype perfectly.

But the daguerreotype also had real drawbacks. Each one was unique: the picture was made directly on the plate, and there was no negative from which to print copies. If you wanted two portraits, you had to sit twice, or someone had to make a daguerreotype of the daguerreotype. The image was also usually reversed left to right, just like a reflection, so a man's coat buttons might appear on the wrong side, and the writing on a sign would appear backwards unless the photographer used a mirror or prism on the camera to flip it.

The surface was fragile too. A finger could wipe the image away, and the silver tarnished if exposed to air. That is why daguerreotypes were kept in small hinged cases made of wood covered with leather or paper, lined with velvet or silk, and sealed behind a glass cover. Later, from the mid-1850s, decorated cases were moulded from a tough early plastic made of shellac and sawdust, called Union cases.

There was a hidden danger, as well. Mercury vapour is poisonous to breathe, and the developing boxes released it into small, poorly ventilated darkrooms. People at the time knew mercury could be harmful, but few took proper precautions, and some daguerreotypists suffered from shaking, headaches and other symptoms of mercury poisoning. Today, museums and modern artists who still make daguerreotypes use careful safety equipment.

By the mid-1850s, cheaper photographs on glass and paper had largely replaced the daguerreotype, as you will see in later parts. Yet for about fifteen years, Daguerre's shining plates were how the world first saw itself in photographs. Daguerre himself retired to the village of Bry-sur-Marne near Paris, where he died on 10 July 1851. His name is one of 72 names of French scientists and engineers engraved around the Eiffel Tower.

There is one more twist in this story. When the news from Paris arrived in England in January 1839, it reached a quiet country house called Lacock Abbey. There, a gentleman scientist named William Henry Fox Talbot had been secretly making pictures with light for years, on paper and by a completely different method. Reading about Daguerre's triumph, Talbot felt a jolt of alarm. Had someone else just beaten him to the greatest invention of his life?

deepDive: What actually happens on a daguerreotype plate? Fuming polished silver with iodine forms a very thin layer of silver iodide, and adding bromine or chlorine creates mixed silver halides that are far more sensitive. When light strikes these crystals, it frees electrons that gather at small defects and reduce a few silver ions to metallic silver atoms. A cluster of just a handful of atoms is enough to form a latent image site. In development, mercury vapour condenses selectively on these sites and forms a silver-mercury amalgam, which builds up into tiny particles a fraction of a micrometre across. These particles scatter light and look white, while the bare polished silver between them reflects like a mirror and looks dark when it reflects a dark surrounding. That is why a daguerreotype flips between positive and negative depending on the viewing angle. Fizeau's gold toning of 1840 coats the particles with gold, strengthening them and warming the tone. The latent image principle was the decisive leap. A direct process like Niépce's bitumen needs light to do all of the chemical work; a developed process lets light do only a tiny amount, which chemistry then multiplies millions of times. This turned exposures of hours into minutes, and later, with brighter lenses such as Petzval's portrait lens of 1840, which had an aperture of about f/3.6 instead of around f/14 or slower, into seconds. Because each f-stop halves or doubles the light, that change in lens alone meant roughly fifteen times more light. Historians debate several points. The broken-thermometer story is widely regarded as a later legend, and letters from 1831–1832 suggest the idea of the iodized silver plate came from Daguerre rather than Niépce, while the debt to Niépce's partnership and earlier work is also clear. Credit for the 'first photograph of a person' depends on definitions: the Boulevard du Temple figure is the earliest verified, though a daguerreotype portrait possibly from 1837 and Bayard's lost self-portraits are sometimes mentioned. Finally, the French state's purchase is often celebrated as an early example of open technology, though the English patent shows the gift was not quite universal.
funFact: Daguerre's Paris street scene of the Boulevard du Temple shows a busy road as almost empty, because every moving carriage and walker vanished during the minutes-long exposure, leaving only a man who stood still to have his boots shined.
